grounds.point: Section 14(1)(b) requires a post-9 June 1952 subletting, assignment or parting with possession without the landlord's consent in writing.
grounds.explanation: The supplied Delhi provision expressly makes the fixed ground depend on a qualifying transfer of the whole or part of the premises on or after 9 June 1952 and the absence of the landlord's written consent. Both the transfer/date element and the written-consent element therefore matter.

grounds.point: The Addl. Rent Controller had found that Respondent No. 1 inducted Respondents No. 2 to 6 under the lease-and-rent-receipt arrangement and that the landlord had consented to the sub-tenancy.
grounds.explanation: The appellate ground itself records that the prior court treated the Lease Deed Ex.PW-1/R-2, Rent Receipt Ex.PW-1/R2-4/1 and other documents as showing landlord consent to the sub-tenancy. That existing finding must be preserved at its stated level even though the appellant challenges its correctness.

grounds.point: The landlord's consent is established to satisfy the statutory requirement of consent in writing for the particular challenged sublettings.
grounds.explanation: The prior court found consent based on written instruments, and the respondents say the lease authorized subletting and the 1977 voucher recorded increased rent on account of subletting. The appellant, however, says the lease required previous written permission and that the receipt was misread; because the supplied record does not reproduce the operative lease clause or voucher text, and the supplied law gives no controlling interpretation of whether these writings constitute the required written consent, their statutory sufficiency cannot be determined.

grounds.point: The relevant subletting or parting transactions to Respondents No. 2 to 6 occurred on or after 9 June 1952.
grounds.explanation: The record says the occupants had been using portions for many years and that Respondents No. 2 to 4 claimed possession before the 10 December 1961 amalgamation, but it supplies no definite creation date for each challenged arrangement. Because section 14(1)(b) expressly uses the 9 June 1952 cutoff, the necessary temporal proposition is not established for all of the alleged transfers.

grounds.point: The Pratap Bank-to-Lakshmi Commercial Bank-to-Canara Bank amalgamations independently establish an actionable assignment under Delhi section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: General Radio applies an Andhra Pradesh statute to a company amalgamation, while its reported Delhi discussion says section 14(b) is broad enough to reach involuntary sale. Telesound gives only a prima facie view concerning amalgamation and expressly reserves whether such vesting amounts to an assignment attracting section 14(1)(b), so the supplied authorities do not conclusively resolve these bank amalgamations under the Delhi provision.

grounds.point: Failure to satisfy the notice regime in sections 17 and 18 by itself establishes the fixed section 14(1)(b) eviction ground.
grounds.explanation: The appellant argued that written consent and notice conditions were necessary for sub-tenant protection, while the respondents disputed the relevance of that argument in this appeal. The supplied statutory text makes lack of written consent part of section 14(1)(b), whereas sections 17 and 18 separately address notice and the consequences for sub-tenants; their text does not make absence of notice a substitute for proving the fixed section 14(1)(b) ground.

reason: The record preserves a prior finding of landlord consent to the sub-tenancies, but the supplied material does not establish whether that consent met the statutory requirement of consent in writing or whether every relevant transfer occurred after the statutory cutoff. The supplied amalgamation authorities also leave the Delhi assignment question unresolved, so the fixed eviction ground cannot be established or definitively defeated on this record.
